docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Ai2-internal only: Beaker access, Docker, and beaker account whoami working.
  • build_image_and_launch.sh refuses to run with uncommitted changes, so commit first.
  • Steps 1–3 run from an open-instruct checkout; step 4 runs from an olmo-eval checkout (uv sync --frozen).

docs.title: 1. Tokenize (CPU job, ~1.5 h)
docs.text:
Training hard-fails if the pre-tokenized cache is missing, so tokenization is a separate job:

./scripts/train/build_image_and_launch.sh scripts/train/debug/oc_sft_olmo3_7b_1node.sh tokenize

The cache key hashes the tokenizer config, mixer, transform functions, max_seq_length and seed. Both jobs read those from shared variables at the top of the script so they cannot drift — if you change one, change it once, and re-tokenize. Any divergence produces a different key and training fails as though tokenization never ran. Never symlink a cache built at a shorter max_seq_length into a longer run's cache path: its rows were truncated at tokenize time and training doesn't check, so the run trains on short data while its config and logs report the long length.

Wait for this job to reach exit 0 before launching step 2.

docs.title: 2. Train (1×8 H100, ~9.5 h)
docs.text:
./scripts/train/build_image_and_launch.sh scripts/train/debug/oc_sft_olmo3_7b_1node.sh train

What a healthy run looks like: 1,723 steps for the epoch, CE from ~1.20 down to ~0.65, smooth, with no instability after the LR peaks around step 52. Step count is a function of the mixture and chat template, not a constant — tokenizer_default resolves to the tokenizer's own template, which prepends a function-calling system block to every conversation without a system message, so rows average 840 tokens rather than the ~643 you get under the olmo_thinker templates.

Checkpoints are written every 345 steps — five per epoch, which is what the eval table below covers — into the directory the job logs as CHECKPOINT_OUTPUT_DIR.

If the job stays queued, run beaker job events <job-id> and read the scheduler's own reason — the two common ones need opposite fixes, and both are spelled out in the script header. Do not guess from cluster docs.

docs.title: 3. Convert checkpoints to HuggingFace
docs.text:
olmo-eval can serve a raw olmo-core checkpoint, but the verified path exports to HF first. One 0-GPU job per checkpoint:

CKPT=<the checkpoint directory the training job wrote to>
STEP=1723
BEAKER_IMAGE=<the image build_image_and_launch.sh printed in step 1>

uv run python mason.py \
    --cluster ai2/saturn ai2/neptune ai2/ceres \
    --workspace ai2/open-instruct-dev \
    --priority urgent \
    --image "$BEAKER_IMAGE" \
    --description "Convert Olmo-3-7B SFT step$STEP -> HF" \
    --pure_docker_mode \
    --num_nodes 1 \
    --gpus 0 \
    --no_auto_dataset_cache \
    -- uv run python scripts/train/convert_olmo_core_to_hf.py \
    --checkpoint-dir $CKPT/step$STEP/model_and_optim \
    --model-name allenai/Olmo-3-1025-7B \
    --tokenizer-name allenai/olmo-3-tokenizer-instruct-dev \
    --output-dir $CKPT/hf_step$STEP

Pass the same tokenizer you trained with. The exported directory carries its chat template, which is what makes the model answer chat-formatted eval prompts at all.

docs.title: 4. Evaluate
docs.text:
From an olmo-eval checkout, one job per checkpoint on 1 GPU (~15 min each). $CKPT and $STEP are the same as in step 3:

uv run olmo-eval beaker launch \
    -n olmo3-7b-sft-step$STEP \
    -m $CKPT/hf_step$STEP \
    -t ifeval_ood -t gsm8k \
    --harness default \
    -o provider.tokenizer=allenai/olmo-3-tokenizer-instruct-dev \
    -c ai2/ceres -c ai2/jupiter \
    -w ai2/open-instruct-dev \
    -B ai2/oe-other \
    -p urgent \
    --no-follow

Evaluate the base model the same way, with -m allenai/Olmo-3-1025-7B, so the delta isolates the weights. ifeval_ood (IFBench, 300 prompts) moves early under instruction tuning and gsm8k (1,319 problems) is the regression check; both are cheap. Swap in a larger suite once you care about a specific claim.

Results print as a Results Summary table at the end of the job log and are written to /results/metrics.json:

checkpoint epoch ifeval_ood gsm8k base Olmo-3-1025-7B 0.00 0.1833 0.7430 step 345 0.20 0.2367 0.7210 step 690 0.40 0.2200 0.7445 step 1035 0.60 0.2133 0.7362 step 1380 0.80 0.2633 0.7597 step 1723 1.00 0.2500 0.7612

Treat differences of a few points as noise: the standard error on an IFBench difference is ~3.5 points at 300 prompts, so the shape of that column is flat after the first checkpoint, and the apparent peak at step 1380 is not separable from sampling variation.

A metric of exactly 0.0000 is a broken run, not a bad model

olmo-eval reports the experiment as Success when every generation request fails. It is almost always a missing chat template — check the -m directory has one, and that provider.tokenizer points at a tokenizer that does.

docs.title: Changing the recipe
docs.text:
• Other base models. --config_name must resolve to an olmo-core TransformerConfig preset; there is no fallback if it does not. Architectures olmo-core has no preset or HF weight conversion for need both written first — see the Olmo-Hybrid report above for what that costs.
  • Other node counts. Hold the global batch at 1,048,576 tokens: per_device × grad_accum × (world_size / cp_degree) × seq_len. Adjust gradient_accumulation_steps, not the sequence length.
  • Verify conversions numerically. If you write or change olmo-core ↔ HF weight conversion, compare a forward pass against the HF reference before training on it. Structural checks — key and shape matching, config round trips, state-dict round trips — all pass cleanly on numerically broken code; in the Olmo-Hybrid work three green CPU checks missed a 38% logit error caused by a single hardcoded epsilon.

docs.title: Synthetic preference dataset
docs.text: This section focuses explicitly on creating synthetic preference datasets.

docs.title: Debug run (use an interactive session)
docs.text:
This code supports HF models, local models and also API-based models (e.g., gpt-4). For generating completions, the code now accepts one model at a time, but we're working on adding an ensemble of models. Stay tuned.

# 1. first sample a bunch of completions given prompts
# Here is an example created dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/vwxyzjn/generation_1725567768
python open_instruct/rejection_sampling/generation.py \
    --dataset_mixer_list HuggingFaceH4/no_robots 100 \
    --dataset_splits train \
    --model_name_or_path allenai/llama-3-tulu-2-8b \
    --num_completions 3 \
    --save_filename output/completions.jsonl \
    --sanity_check \
    --push_to_hub

docs.title: Create preference pairs
docs.text:
# 2.1 do LLM as a judge to create synthetic preference dataset
# Here is an example created dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/vwxyzjn/synthetic_preference_dataset_1725567862
python open_instruct/rejection_sampling/synthetic_preference_dataset.py \
    --input_filename output/completions.jsonl \
    --model gpt-4o-2024-08-06 \
    --save_filename output/synthetic_preferences.jsonl \
    --num_completions 3 \
    --push_to_hub \

You can visualize the dataset via

python -m costa_utils.hf_viz \
    --sft vwxyzjn/synthetic_preference_dataset_1725567862 \
    --split train \
    --sft_messages_column_name whole_conversation

python -m costa_utils.hf_viz \
    --preference vwxyzjn/synthetic_preference_dataset_1725567862 \
    --split train \
    --preference_chosen_column_name chosen \
    --preference_rejected_column_name rejected

docs.title: Run through the entire dataset run
docs.text:
To run through the entire dataset you would need a lot more GPUs to finish the generation more quickly.

# NOTE: the scripts below only generate 400 prompts, so it's for demonstration purposes only. The scripts are highly scalable, and you could modify its `num_prompts=400` to something else like 300000 for the tulu dataset.

# you need to make sure your default beaker workspace has WANDB_API_KEY and HF_TOKEN secrets in them
beaker secret write HF_TOKEN xxxxxxxxxxxx
beaker secret write WANDB_API_KEY xxxxxxxxxxx

# Docker mode: using caches from WEKA
deploy_mode="docker_weka" bash scripts/synthetic_preference_dataset.bash

# Docker mode: using caches from NFS
deploy_mode="docker_nfs" bash scripts/synthetic_preference_dataset.bash

# Docker mode: do not use caches
deploy_mode="docker" bash scripts/synthetic_preference_dataset.bash

# If you have environment setup with NFS and want to launch debug mode:
deploy_mode="nfs" bash scripts/synthetic_preference_dataset.bash

You can see a demo here

docs.title: Training Tool-Using Models and RL Environments
docs.text:
This page is for people who want to train models in Open-Instruct that do more than produce a single final answer. You can use it to:

  • train a model to call tools such as Python, web search, browsing, or MCP servers
  • train against stateful RL environments such as guessing games or Wordle
  • combine intermediate environment rewards with a final verifier-based reward

The recommended workflow is user-facing and script-first: start from an existing debug or training script, choose the tool or environment setup you want, then adjust the configuration for your dataset and infrastructure. You should not need to build a new training loop just to add tool use.

Right now, Open-Instruct supports a simple interaction model where environment outputs are appended back into the conversation during multi-turn GRPO rollouts.

docs.title: Example Scripts
docs.text:
Start from one of these scripts. They are the fastest way to see the expected config shape and get a working run before customizing anything.

Script Description scripts/train/debug/tools/qwen3_vllm_hermes_parser_debug.sh Train a model to call common tools with a standard chat-style parser scripts/train/debug/tools/mcp_weather_debug.sh Train a model against tools exposed by an MCP server scripts/train/debug/tools/dr_tulu_parser_debug.sh Reproduce a DR-Tulu-style tool-calling setup scripts/train/debug/envs/guess_number_1gpu.sh Train against a built-in tool-style environment scripts/train/debug/envs/wordle_8gpu.sh Train against a built-in text environment. This uses mason to launch, so non-AI2 users will likely need to adapt the launcher.

docs.title: Quick Parameter Overview
docs.text:
These are the main parameters you will usually touch when enabling tools or environments:

Parameter What it controls Typical use --tools Which tools or environments are active for the run --tools python serper_search. Look at TOOL_REGISTRY for the full list. --tool_call_names The names the model sees and emits when calling those tools, in the order matching --tools. --tool_call_names code search --tool_configs Per-tool or per-environment settings, set globally for the run. e.g.API endpoints, MCP server info, timeouts, environment defaults. Again, order must match --tools. --tool_configs {'api_key': '1234567890'} {} --tool_parser_type How model output is parsed into tool calls. See Parsers for more details. Use vllm_* unless you know what you are doing. --tool_parser_type vllm_hermes --max_steps Maximum number of tool/environment interaction steps per rollout. --max_steps 200 --per_turn_max_tokens Optional per-turn token limit for each tool/environment interaction step. Useful if you want to allow many interactions (large overall response length) but limit amount of tokens per step. --per_turn_max_tokens 1024 --pass_tools_to_chat_template By default true, but you can turn it off if you have a custom system prompt or parser that already provides information about the tools. --pass_tools_to_chat_template True --pool_size Number of worker actors per tool or environment. Increase if tool calls are becoming a bottleneck. Controls how many concurrent tool/environment interactions can run at once (e.g. useful for rate limits). By default, this is set to the number of rollouts per batch (num_rollouts_per_batch * num_unique_prompts_rollout). --pool_size 16 --reward_aggregator How per-step rewards are combined across the rollout. Can be last (just take the last step's reward) or sum (add up all step rewards). --reward_aggregator sum

docs.title: How the Rollout Works
docs.text:
At a high level, a tool- or environment-enabled rollout looks like this:

  1. Open-Instruct builds the prompt from your dataset example.
  2. The model generates one turn of text.
  3. The parser either extracts a structured tool call or forwards the full text to a text environment.
  4. The selected tool or environment returns a StepResult.
  5. The StepResult.result text is formatted and appended back into the conversation.
  6. Training continues until the rollout hits max_steps or a step returns done=True.
  7. Per-step rewards are aggregated with --reward_aggregator, then combined with any final verifier reward.

The key implementation idea is that you configure the rollout from the script layer, while Open-Instruct handles the multi-turn dispatch loop underneath.

docs.title: Optional search backend: You.com (you_search)
docs.text:
you_search is an optional alternative to serper_search. It takes the same query argument and formats results the same way (title, snippet text, source URL).

  • Configuration: set YDC_API_KEY to a You.com API key and pass --tools you_search. num_results (default 5) and timeout (default 10 seconds) can be set through the tool config, as with Serper. If YDC_API_KEY is unset, the tool raises a configuration error when it is created.
  • API: requests go to the keyed Search API, POST https://ydc-index.io/v1/search, with the key in the X-API-Key header. There is no keyless fallback.
  • Usage costs: keyed requests are billed per You.com's pricing. See you.com/platform for current rates and credits. Every tool call during rollouts is a billed request.
  • Attribution: requests to You.com send User-Agent: youdotcom-integration/allenai-open-instruct so You.com can attribute the traffic. The header is set only on requests to You.com, not on other tools' traffic.

docs.title: Adding Your Own Tools or Environments
docs.text:
When adding your own tool or environment, there are three potential options:

Class Description Tool A stateless tool that can be called by the model. You only need to implement the step method. RLEnvironment A stateful environment that can be used to train a model. You need to implement the reset and step methods. Interfaces with the model via tool/function calling. TextRLEnvironment A stateful environment that receives the model's full generation at each step. Use this when you want custom parsing or reward logic without relying on structured tool calls. In practice, subclasses implement _reset and text_step.

As a rule of thumb:

  • use Tool for stateless request/response integrations like Python execution or web search.
  • use RLEnvironment for stateful tasks where the model acts through tool/function calls, e.g. a docker sandbox.
  • use TextRLEnvironment when the environment should inspect the model's raw text directly, e.g. proper multi-turn training with a simulated user.

reset is primarily for environment setup and returns the initial StepResult plus tool definitions. For stateless tools, the default reset implementation mainly exposes the tool schema.

Note that behind the scenes, Open-Instruct creates a worker pool for each tool or environment, and passes the config fields into the constructor. As such, each rollout gets a fresh instance of the tool or environment, and so you can store state inside the tool or environment object if you want!

After this, you need to add a config class for your tool or environment for any runtime parameters that are not part of the EnvCall interface!

docs.title: Config classes and how config wiring works
docs.text:
Each tool or environment is paired with a config dataclass that subclasses BaseEnvConfig. In practice, this is the object that holds the fixed settings for that tool or environment, such as API endpoints, timeouts, or game parameters.

These config elements can have defaults, be set globally for a run, and/or be overridden per-sample in the dataset. This can be useful if you want to use the same tool or environment with different settings for different samples.

docs.title: tool_name vs tool_call_name
docs.text:
By default, the name you pass in --tools is also the name the model uses when calling that tool. You can override the model-facing name with --tool_call_names.

For example:

--tools python serper_search \
--tool_call_names code search

In that case:

  • Open-Instruct looks up python and serper_search in the registry, and creates environments using the corresponding classes.
  • the model sees and calls code and search in its function calling interface.

This can be useful if you want to swap tool backends without changing the name the model uses, or if you want the tool names in training to better match some external setup you are reproducing.

docs.title: How tool definitions are exposed to the model
docs.text:
Tool definitions are the OpenAI-style function schemas returned by get_tool_definitions(). Open-Instruct collects these definitions from the active tool or environment pools and uses them in two places:

  • to tell the parser which function names and argument schemas are valid
  • to pass tool schemas into the chat template when --pass_tools_to_chat_template is enabled

This is the main connection between tools and environments: both ultimately expose tool definitions to the model, even if the underlying implementation is stateful.

For a plain Tool, get_tool_definitions() usually exposes a single function schema. For a stateful RLEnvironment, get_tool_definitions() can expose one or more actions the model may take. For TextRLEnvironment, reset() returns no tool definitions, because the model interacts through raw text instead of function calls.

For example, if you configure:

--tools python \
--tool_call_names code

then the model is shown a function definition named code, not python. If your dataset uses per-sample tools filtering, those entries should also use code, because that is the function name exposed to the model.

docs.title: Subclass implementation details
docs.text:
The step interface takes an EnvCall object, which contains:

  • name: the tool or action name
  • args: a keyword dict containing parsed arguments

These arguments should follow the OpenAI function calling spec, so in practice you should stick to JSON-serializable types.

The step method returns a StepResult, which contains the fields that matter during training:

  • result: the observation text appended back into the conversation
  • reward: the per-step reward
  • done: whether the rollout should terminate early
  • metadata: optional debugging or runtime information

The reward is stored per turn and then aggregated at the end of the rollout depending on --reward_aggregator. If done=True, generation stops immediately.

docs.title: Text environment implementation note
docs.text:
TextRLEnvironment has a slightly different contract than Tool or RLEnvironment. Instead of receiving a parsed tool call from the model, it receives the model's full text output. Internally, Open-Instruct wraps that text into a synthetic EnvCall under args["text"] and forwards it to text_step.

This is why text environments are the right fit when:

  • the model should emit plain text rather than strict tool calls
  • the environment needs to do its own parsing
  • reward depends on text format or multi-turn text behavior

docs.title: Minimal implementation sketch
docs.text:
For most custom integrations, the required surface is intentionally small:

class MyEnv(RLEnvironment):
    async def reset(self, **kwargs):
        return StepResult(result="initial observation"), tool_definitions

    async def step(self, call: EnvCall):
        return StepResult(result="next observation", reward=0.0, done=False)

For a text environment:

class MyTextEnv(TextRLEnvironment):
    async def _reset(self, **kwargs):
        return StepResult(result="")

    async def text_step(self, text: str):
        return StepResult(result="feedback", reward=0.0, done=False)

docs.title: Parsers
docs.text:
Parsers are responsible for handling text formatting: both extracting tool calls from the model generation (either to call tools or to interact with environments) and formatting environment observations back into the conversation. We support three types of parsers right now:

Parser Description legacy XML-tag prompts within the assistant turn. Expects <tool_name>...</tool_name>; only passes the string inside to the tool. vllm_* Wrapper around vLLM's native parsers. Uses native vLLM parsing to extract tool calls, and then wraps to add observation formatting. We support vllm_hermes, vllm_llama3_json, vllm_olmo3, and vllm_qwen3xml, and it should be easy to add more. dr_tulu Wrapper around the dr_agent_mcp tool for DR-Tulu-style tool calling.

We recommend using vllm_* parsers unless you have a strong reason for using another parser.

docs.title: Example Script: Wordle
docs.text:
The scripts/train/debug/envs/wordle_8gpu.sh script is a good example of how to train against a built-in text environment. It uses the vllm_hermes parser together with the WordleTextEnv class. The environment handles parsing guesses, generating feedback, and assigning rewards. Over 200 steps, the training curves should look something like this:

You can see the wandb for this run here and the beaker link here.

docs.title: Example Script: DR Tulu
docs.text:
./scripts/train/dr-tulu/dr_tulu_qwen35.sh provides a script to replicate DR Tulu training with some differences: using Qwen3.5-9B as the starting model and using the model's existing tool calling parameters instead of a custom parser.

For rubric-based training, you can enable evolving rubrics with: 

--apply_evolving_rubric_reward true \
--max_active_rubrics 5 \
--max_active_rubrics controls how many rubrics are active for a given prompt at once. You can save the generated evolving rubrics by setting --cache_evolving_rubric_data_dir to a folder path. Note that the verifer should be set to rubric for use with evolving rubrics.

For the evolving rubrics, you can set the judge and generation model with RUBRIC_JUDGE_MODEL, RUBRIC_GENERATION_MODEL respectively. Both use litellm to interface with providers, so you can use openai, vllm, etc.

docs.title: Running SFT on TPU: a known-good starting point
docs.text:
Olmo 3.5 small (the 4T EMO base) on Dolci-Think with H045's recipe, on one TPU v4 4x4x8 slice (128 chips) of the gke-tpu-v4 cluster, through MaxText + Tunix.

Measured cost and outcome: 11,768 steps of 16 × 65,536 tokens at a median 3.94 s/step, 13.5 h wall clock from submit to the last step. The loss matches H045's GPU runs (parity windows in open-instruct#1933). The GPU recipe takes 5 h 54 m on 2×8 H100, so the TPU path is slower per run. Its advantage is capacity: four of these runs fit at once without touching Beaker.

The recipe is scripts/tpu/maxtext/k8s/olmo35-sft-4x4x8/. Its kustomization.yaml header records why each setting is what it is; read it before editing. Olmo 3 7B has its own overlay, k8s/instruct-sft-4x4x8/; its base k8s/olmo3-sft/ targets a 2x2x4 slice, which no longer exists. scripts/tpu/maxtext/README.md lists the MaxText patches.

docs.title: Example runs
docs.text: Run What it is olmo35-sft-h045-tpu-full-r2 This recipe, verbatim: the TPU replica of the ledger's H045 anchor (arm anchor-emo-olmo35-tpu). 0 restarts, final CE 0.9245. HF export: /weka/oe-adapt-default/abhishekr/tpu-posttrain/hf/olmo35-sft-h045-tpu-full-r2-step11768. H067, H072 (olmo-post-training-ledger) The same recipe with other data: arms, seeds, resumes and their checks are recorded in those hypothesis files and in open-instruct#1976 and #1977.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• IAM on the ai2-olmo GCP project, e.g. roles/container.developer.
  • A network the cluster accepts. allenai/olmo-gcp-infra's README lists them: the office IPs, its Tailscale exit nodes, and Beaker sessions on ai2/hammond. From anywhere else, use the DNS endpoint (--dns-endpoint). Then:
gcloud container clusters get-credentials gke-tpu-v4 --zone us-central2-b --project ai2-olmo
kubectl -n olmo get workloads

kubectl needs gke-gcloud-auth-plugin (gcloud components install gke-gcloud-auth-plugin, or a binary in ~/.local/bin). - gcloud logins expire about daily, and kubectl then fails quietly. Watchers go blind without an error. Agents use the service account tpu-posttrain-agent@ai2-olmo.iam.gserviceaccount.com: export CLOUDSDK_CORE_ACCOUNT to it in every process, background watchers included. Move ~/.kube/gke_gcloud_auth_plugin_cache aside when switching identity, or kubectl keeps the cached one. People log in with their own account. - Agents. Claude Code and Codex in this repo load a summary of this guide's rules from the tpu skill. Update it when you change a rule here. - Where things live. Everything is in us-central2. Data, tokenizers and checkpoints are in gs://ai2-olmo-dev/post-training/, and the nodes mount its data/ and tokenizers/ subfolders, each on its own, under /mnt/post-training through gcsfuse. Never mount a folder that holds checkpoints: the metadata prefetch lists all of it on every host at every pod start (k8s/narrow_mounts.py narrows an overlay). Images are in us-docker.pkg.dev/ai2-olmo/olmo/maxtext-posttrain.

docs.title: What the cluster is
docs.text:
gke-tpu-v4 holds 4,096 reserved v4 chips at 4 per host. Since 2026-10-21 they are cut into seven 4x4x8 slices (128 chips) and three 8x8x16 (1,024), with 128 chips held back so GKE can auto-repair failed nodes; the 8x8x8 is gone. The layout changes as the cluster's admins reslice it, so check it before planning: kubectl get nodes -L cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool --no-headers | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c (32 hosts per 4x4x8, 256 per 8x8x16). A slice runs one job at a time. Kueue admits jobs from four queues in one cohort:

Queue Who Preempted by hero the main pretraining run; owns all the quota nothing dev tests hero post-training, data-adaptation us; share what is left hero, dev

Use post-training. Its jobs run on borrowed quota and are preempted whenever hero or dev needs the slice, so checkpoint often enough to lose little. Never hold a slice in a way that delays hero.

The recipe needs exactly a 4x4x8: its mesh puts one 64K row on 8 chips, so 128 chips hold its 16 rows. The measurements below on the former 8x8x8 ran the same mesh at 64 rows per step, which is a different recipe (H078's 4x batch). On the former 8x8x8, the measured 16-row configuration used olmo35-cp-ep, splitting each row 32 ways and changing the MoE load-balance term. No validated 16-row configuration for the 8x8x16 is documented here. Measured meshes are in Changing the recipe.

docs.title: Cost per slice
docs.text:
From TensorBoard perf/*. Throughput is tokens per chip-second: tokens per device per step divided by the mean step time over steps 31-100, so a stalled step counts at its full cost.

slice config rows/step median s/step tokens/s/chip steps over 3x median 4x4x8 the recipe (A0') 16 3.88 2,055 0 8x8x8 H078's config, with the data-order shim (H088 opt-a) 64 4.28 1,386 4.3% (13% over H078's whole runs) 8x8x8 same, no shim and no batch hashes (H088 opt-b) 64 4.23 1,887 0 8x8x8 opt-b + remat_policy=save_dot_except_mlp (H088 opt-c) 64 4.18 1,900 0; a tie, keep full

Startup before step 1 (pods, restore, an 11-12 min compile) adds 20-35 min on either slice, paid again at every resume.

  • Use a 4x4x8 for this recipe. Among the measured configurations it used the fewest chip-hours per token; no throughput is measured here for the 8x8x16, which is hero's and borrowed only. The 8x8x8 was split into 4x4x8s on 2026-10-21, so the 8x8x8 results below are historical. The 8x8x8 overlay is k8s/olmo35-sft-8x8x8/: the same token budget at 64 rows and 2,942 steps. Its data order differs from the 4x4x8 recipe's, so an arm on it needed a control on the same slice and config. Without the shim the 8x8x8 is projected at ~1.09x the chip-hours of the 4x4x8, finishing a run ~3.6x sooner (H088, allenai/open-instruct#2020). This is a steady-state projection, not a measured cost. Both rates come from stall-free 70-step windows on different days (4x4x8 10-14, 8x8x8 10-18). The 8x8x8's stall rate over a whole run without the shim is not measured. The 8x8x8 could not run the 16-row recipe at that rate (see Changing the recipe).
  • Historical 8x8x8 input stalls. H088 removed the data-order shim (MAXTEXT_R2_DATA_EMULATION) and MAXTEXT_LOG_BATCH_HASH=1 together, so their separate contributions are not isolated. With both, one step in eight stalled for 20-35 s, at the same steps in every run, and H078's runs cost 1.8-1.9x the chip-hours of a 4x4x8. In xprof the stall is one host's input pipeline (grain process_prefetch waiting 29 s) while every TPU waits for its batch in jit__device_put_reshard. The HF input pipeline allows at most one grain worker, so more workers are not a fix.
  • Keep remat_policy=full. Saving dot outputs except the MLP's gained 0.7%, with the same loss.
  • Outside stalls a step is ~4.0 s of device compute and ~0.2-0.5 s idle. FSDP all-gather waits are ~16% of the compute, and num_vocab_tiling=16 costs ~4% (the 205 MB embedding is all-gathered and its gradient all-reduced 96 times a step).
  • Both slices run at ~4% of v4's 275 TFLOP/s bf16 peak by MaxText's own FLOP count.
  • jax memory_stats() peaks (0.9-2.3 GiB) leave out XLA temporaries: the same 8x8x8 config needed 32.17 GB at compile with ragged_buffer_factor=4.0. Read HBM headroom from the compile error or xprof, not from those lines.

docs.title: 1. Image
docs.text:
us-docker.pkg.dev/ai2-olmo/olmo/maxtext-posttrain:51f8cc4b-p907d86f3-rfb46e215e

This tag is r2's image (51f8cc4b-p907d86f3, built from image-olmo35/) plus image-olmo35-rf/. That patch adds a fix for resuming from a checkpoint (without it, restore runs out of HBM) and batch-hash logging. Training numerics are unchanged: a replay produced bit-identical CE and 9,952 of 9,952 equal batch hashes. This is the default image for the recipe above. The optional pooled resume image includes additional patches; its parity checks compare against its own base image. The Olmo 3 image is built by image/build.sh <maxtext commit>.

To build a new image, run build.sh from any host with gcloud (a Beaker session works). Cloud Build carries the context base64-encoded inside the build config. Builds use Cloud Build's default service account. Set BUILD_SERVICE_ACCOUNT to a full projects/<project>/serviceAccounts/<email> resource only when the caller is authorized to use that account.

docs.title: 2. Base checkpoint
docs.text:
The loader reads an Orbax parameter tree (…/0/items) from GCS.

  • Olmo 3.5 (OLMo-core distcp). This runs in two stages, on CPU:
python scripts/tpu/maxtext/olmo35/dump_olmocore_masters.py <step dir> <masters dir>              # needs olmo_core
python scripts/tpu/maxtext/olmo35/convert_olmocore_to_maxtext.py <step dir> <masters dir> <out>   # needs maxtext
gcloud storage cp -r <out>/0 gs://ai2-olmo-dev/post-training/checkpoints/<name>/

It keeps OLMo-core's padded 100,352 vocabulary, whose padded rows were trained. The 4T EMO base is already at gs://ai2-olmo-dev/post-training/checkpoints/olmo35-small-4t-emo-step5961/0/items. - Olmo 3 (HF). Use MaxText's converter with model_name=olmo3-7b. olmo3-7b-pt has no YaRN, so it is wrong for the 1025 base.

JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu python -m maxtext.checkpoint_conversion.to_maxtext model_name=olmo3-7b base_output_directory=<out> \
  scan_layers=True use_multimodal=false hardware=cpu skip_jax_distributed_system=true \
  checkpoint_storage_use_zarr3=1 checkpoint_storage_use_ocdbt=1 --hf_model_path=allenai/Olmo-3-1025-7B --save_dtype=bfloat16

Check any new conversion numerically against the source model before training on it. Key and shape checks pass on broken conversions.

docs.title: 3. Data and tokenizer
docs.text:
MaxText streams parquet files. Its shuffle only permutes files and mixes a small buffer, and hub shards are grouped by source, so shuffle globally first. olmo35/build_full_dolci_think.py (Olmo 3.5) and data/build_full_dolci.py (Olmo 3) write N shuffled shards from one dataset revision and use the standard HF cache settings. Pin the input with --revision <dataset commit>, or use --data-files '<local parquet glob>' for local files; the output directory must be new or empty. Upload the shards to gs://ai2-olmo-dev/post-training/data/<name>/. Ledger experiments shard each arm and seed into 512 files with experiments/h067/shard.py in olmo-post-training-ledger.

The tokenizer is a directory on the bucket. For Olmo 3.5, olmo35/tok_oi35.py saves H045's tokenizer and template (allenai/dolma2-tokenizer-olmo35 @8b971706, olmo35). For Olmo 3, save PreTrainedTokenizerFast.from_pretrained("allenai/olmo-3-tokenizer-instruct-dev") (see Traps).

docs.title: 4. Launch
docs.text:
Copy k8s/olmo35-sft-4x4x8/ to a new directory. Then rename the JobSet and both ConfigMaps (in jobset.yaml and kustomization.yaml) to a new unique name, and edit the env block:

Variable Meaning RUN_NAME, OUTPUT_DIR Checkpoints go to $OUTPUT_DIR/$RUN_NAME/checkpoints/<step>/. LOAD_PARAMETERS_PATH, TOKENIZER_PATH, TRAIN_FILES Step 2 and step 3 outputs (/mnt/post-training/... = gs://ai2-olmo-dev/post-training/...). TOTAL_DEVICES, GLOBAL_BATCH, PER_DEVICE_BATCH 128 chips × 0.125 = 16 sequences per step, with no gradient accumulation. The launcher derives accumulation and fails if the numbers don't divide. SEQ_LEN 65,536. Tokens per step = GLOBAL_BATCH × SEQ_LEN. STEPS, LR_SCHEDULE_STEPS Steps trained, and the horizon the LR decays over (warmup WARMUP_FRAC of it). Set STEPS below the horizon to run the start of a longer recipe, e.g. for a loss-parity check. NUM_EPOCH Passes the stream holds. STEPS decides what is trained; a pass shorter than STEPS repeats data. EXTRA_ARGS MaxText flags. The mesh is custom_mesh_and_rule=olmo35-ep-as-cp ici_fsdp_parallelism=16 ici_expert_parallelism=8: batch over FSDP, and the expert axis doubles as context parallelism outside the MoE. checkpoint_period and max_num_checkpoints_to_keep set what is saved. images: newTag The image tag from step 1. 
kubectl --context gke_ai2-olmo_us-central2-b_gke-tpu-v4 apply -k <your overlay dir>
kubectl -n olmo get workloads              # ADMITTED True = it has a slice
kubectl -n olmo get jobset <name>          # TERMINALSTATE, RESTARTS, SUSPENDED (a hero preemption suspends it)
kubectl -n olmo get pods -l jobset.sigs.k8s.io/jobset-name=<name>

To stop a run, deactivate its Kueue workload: kubectl -n olmo patch $(kubectl -n olmo get workloads -o name | grep "/jobset-<name>-") --type merge -p '{"spec":{"active":false}}'. Setting the JobSet's spec.suspend does nothing while Kueue has it admitted: Kueue resets it, and a watcher that relied on it left a run training on the 8x8x8 for 4.5 h after its stop rule fired.

Startup takes ~35 min: the 32 pods start a few minutes after admission, then the model compiles and the first step runs. k8s/watch_jobset.sh <jobset> <run> [max minutes] saves every pod's log when the JobSet ends. Pod logs vanish once the JobSet is deleted or restarted, so save them before either.

docs.title: 5. Read the loss
docs.text:
Read the step loss only from the LOSS-PARTS step=N ce=… moe_lb=… z=… tokens=… line, which one pod logs. Each pod's completed step: N, … loss: line is that pod's own value: on one step the 32 pods ranged 1.28–1.68. Compare ce= with H045's train/CE loss, never Tunix's loss, which adds the MoE load-balancing and z-losses.

A healthy Olmo 3.5 run: REQUIRED_RBF (the MoE buffer factor that would have dropped no token) stays below the configured ragged_buffer_factor=2.5. r2's maximum was 2.24.

REQUIRED_RBF is logged every step by JAX process 0 only, and that is often not pod slice-0-0: find the pod whose log has it. Kubelet keeps about 700 steps of each pod's log, and the agent service account cannot read Cloud Logging. So if a rule needs every step's value, stream that pod with kubectl logs -f from step 1. A watcher polling kubectl logs every 5 minutes lost 14 steps at one rotation (H078 bb4-lr1e4-s0), and the run had to be relaunched.

docs.title: 6. Checkpoints, preemption and resume
docs.text:
• enable_checkpointing=true is required even if you want no checkpoints. Without it, jax.distributed is never initialised on multi-host TPU and Tunix crashes.
  • Tunix always saves the final step. An Olmo 3.5 checkpoint with optimizer state is ~137 GB. Agents delete nothing on GCS; ask the run's owner.
  • After a preemption, JobSet restarts the run from the last checkpoint, on the same overlay. A resume replays the data pipeline to the restored step at ~1.4 s per skipped batch, which is hours late in a run. Resume only on the restore-fix image (step 1), or a derivative that includes that fix, such as the pooled image below.

scripts/tpu/maxtext/image-olmo35-fs/ adds an optional spawned worker pool for the SFT chat-template map. The published image is:

us-docker.pkg.dev/ai2-olmo/olmo/maxtext-posttrain:51f8cc4b-p907d86f3-rfb46e215e-bs3ec936c3-dc88c6c7ea-fse2555fa0

It includes the restore fix and these MaxText fork changes:

Image layer Fork revisions Changes bs3ec936c3 c469d980 → 736b296c Big-slice mesh support, KDA sharding constraints, and optional r2 data-order emulation. dc88c6c7ea 736b296c → 1e612a76 Optional MoE dropped-token logging, including the dropless fallback correction. fse2555fa0 1e612a76 → e0e1c2a9 Pooled chat-template map; unset or zero workers keeps the serial map.

The bs and dc build recipes are not included here; build.sh depends on the published ...-dc88c6c7ea base. For a late 4x4x8 resume of a run already using that base, set images[].newTag to the part after : above and add MAXTEXT_SFT_TEMPLATE_WORKERS=32 to your recipe's environment ConfigMap (configMapGenerator[].literals in your copied kustomization.yaml, named olmo35-sft-env in the 4x4x8 example). Here 32 is the tested worker count per data-loading process, not a tuned optimum. The pool stays active during training as well as replay; leave it unset for fresh starts and short resumes unless measured input-pipeline savings justify its ~4-6 min startup cost. Steady-state TPU training gains have not been measured.

Validation against the same ...-dc88c6c7ea base: 10,000 rows identical on CPU, including file and epoch boundaries; on TPU, 2,144 of 2,144 batch hashes and steps 61-66 CE equal the serial resume. The CPU map was ~10x faster, but the 60-step TPU replay took 366 s pooled versus 63 s serial because of startup. Long-resume TPU throughput is still unmeasured. The checked-in examples use older images (...-rfb46e215e or ...-bs3ec936c3); these checks do not establish parity when migrating them, since that also adds the layers above. Validate batches and CE against the run's current image before migrating those runs.

docs.title: 7. Export to HF and evaluate
docs.text:
gcloud storage cp -r gs://ai2-olmo-dev/post-training/runs/<run>/checkpoints/<step>/model_params <local dir>
python scripts/tpu/maxtext/olmo35/export_maxtext_to_hf.py <local dir>/model_params <reference HF dir> <out>

The reference directory supplies tensor names, config.json, modeling code, tokenizer and chat template. Use an HF export of the same model with the matching tokenizer and chat template, and choose <out> under your own output location. One existing reference export is H045's: /weka/oe-training-default/ai2-llm/checkpoints/abhishekr/hero-sft-4t/runs/h045-anchor-emo-olmo35-s34521/hf_step11768. Its config.json is the HF model config, unlike the run directory's OLMo-core training config. The exporter is bit-exact on all 23,441 tensors. For Olmo 3, use export_hf.sh, which also takes the base model's config.json, because MaxText's own is wrong.

Evaluate the HF export with olmo-eval on Beaker GPUs, as for a GPU run (see the GPU guide). HF Olmo 3.5 needs fla, so every pass runs on GPU. Where exports and checkpoints go, and what to keep, is the ledger's storage skill (olmo-post-training-ledger skills/storage/SKILL.md).

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
Each of these trained silently on wrong data or a wrong model before it was found.

  • Dropped EOS targets. Olmo tokenizers have bos == eos, and MaxText's target shift ignored BOS targets, so SFT never learned to stop while the loss looked fine. Fixed in the image. Check P(EOS) after an answer on any new pipeline.
  • YaRN. Olmo 3 applies YaRN to full-attention layers only. Unpatched MaxText also applies it to sliding-window layers, which costs +0.1 nats/token at the start. Fixed in the image.
  • Vocab padding. 100,278 isn't divisible by tensor parallelism. Zero-padding to 100,352 is wrong (+3.2 nats/token). Replicate the vocab axis instead: logical_axis_rules=[['vocab',[]],['activation_vocab',[]]].
  • Olmo 3 tokenizer. allenai/olmo-3-tokenizer-instruct-dev loads as GPT2Tokenizer under transformers 5 and drops the pre-tokenizer. Train with a PreTrainedTokenizerFast save.
  • KDA miscompile on v4. Slicing a reshape inside the sub-block inverse dropped a column offset on TPU only (CPU was correct). Fixed in maxtext 9f55e7b6 (in the image). Kernel rewrites need a TPU-vs-exact-scan check, not only a CPU one.
  • MoE buffer. Fully dropless runs out of HBM at 64K. ragged_buffer_factor=2.5 drops nothing as long as REQUIRED_RBF stays below it.
  • Restore OOM. r2's image replicates the expert Adam moments on restore and runs out of HBM. Use the restore-fix image.
  • Data order depends on slice shape. Batches are packed per data host, so a different host count gives a different, still valid, data order. Keep every arm of a comparison, and its control, on the same slice shape.
  • Context parallelism with load balancing gives a wrong forward. With ici_context_parallelism > 1 and MaxText's default context_parallel_load_balance=True, dense Olmo 3 7B's step-1 CE on a fixed packed batch was off by +0.39 (cp4) and +1.98 (cp8) against an HF forward; cp4 with context_parallel_load_balance=False matches it (0.919794 vs 0.919799). The suspected cause, from the code, is that the SFT input path never applies the load-balancing reorder that attention then assumes; upstream confirmation is pending. Turn load balancing off, and check step-1 LOSS-PARTS CE against an HF forward of the same batch before trusting any new mesh. The recipe's olmo35-ep-as-cp uses the expert axis rather than ici_context_parallelism; on Olmo 3.5 small its step-1 CE matched an HF forward of the same 64 rows (1.077855 vs 1.077850).
  • Zero steps, exit 0. train_sft exits 0 with no steps when the data iterator fails. The launcher's step guard catches it; keep that guard.
  • KDA all-gathers on a new mesh. Under olmo35-cp-ep on the 8x8x8, the KDA chunk scan's inputs and states were sharded on the chunk axis, so XLA all-gathered them inside every scan iteration: 97.6% of a 475 s step. Logical constraints in _delta_rule_chunked_subblock (abhishekraok/maxtext c5f1251d) bring the step to 3.33 s. CPU runs never show in-loop gathers, so profile one TPU step with xprof before trusting a new mesh.
  • Compile-time HBM. At 64 rows on the 8x8x8, ragged_buffer_factor=4.0 failed to compile (HLO temporaries 32.17 GB vs 31.75 GB of HBM); 3.0 compiles, and the runs peaked at 2.39-2.84.
  • GCS egress quota. Two big slices loading the base checkpoint at once hit google_egress_bandwidth (us-central2) and failed at startup. Stagger big-slice launches.
  • The control host is a single point of failure. Watchers and log tailers die with the host they run on (a Beaker session lost its node on 2026-10-16). Keep any record a rule depends on in a source that survives it.
  • hostNetwork. The image's libtpu forms a multi-host slice only on the host network. Keep hostNetwork: true and dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet.
  • pgrep -f / pkill -f inside bash -c match their own command line: loops never end and kills hit the caller. Use PIDs.

docs.title: Changing the recipe
docs.text:
• Other slice sizes and meshes. olmo35-ep-as-cp puts one 64K row on 8 chips (KDA's 8 heads). Measured on Olmo 3.5 small with 65,536-token rows:
slice mesh rows/step s/step tokens/s/chip status 4x4x8 olmo35-ep-as-cp, fsdp 16 x expert 8 16 3.94 2,080 r2 and A0'; the recipe 8x8x8 olmo35-ep-as-cp, fsdp 64 x expert 8 64 4.28 1,910 H078's 4x batch; ragged_buffer_factor=3.0; 1,887 tokens/s/chip without the shim, see Cost 8x8x8 olmo35-cp-ep + c5f1251d 16 3.33 620 runs, but numerics differ from the 4x4x8 (#1933) 8x8x16 olmo35-cp-ep, fsdp 64 x context 2 x expert 8 64 - - never reached step 1 (egress quota, then a TPU core halt)

Each mesh was picked to keep r2's per-device layout, not tuned. No sweep of the parallelism split, remat policy or per-device batch has been run, so these are known-good points, not optima. Any other slice or mesh needs its own same-slice control. - Comparing against a GPU result. TPU and GPU runs of the same recipe differ in data order and numerics. Compare TPU arms with a TPU control on the same slice shape.

docs.title: Trained Model Location
docs.text:
When running our training scripts, the model will get uploaded to several places when applicable for redundancy, depending on the cluster environment:

  • Hugging Face
  • Google Cloud Storage
  • Ai2's internal beaker dataset
  • Local storage

docs.title: Ai2 Internal Setup
docs.text: This document details some best practices when working with our cluster.

docs.title: (One-time setup) VScode + Weka setup
docs.text:
You should join the #vscode-weka-dev-workflow slack channel to setup your VScode to work with weka.

After following the instructions there, you should end up with a VScode / Cursor setup that looks like this:

  • Your terminal has direct access to the weka filesystem.
  • You can run beaker commands from the terminal.
  • You can edit files in the weka filesystem.
  • You can run python scripts with the pyenv / uv environment.

docs.title: (One-time setup) Setup API keys
docs.text:
You need to first obtain API key or tokens from the following website:

  • BEAKER_TOKEN: https://beaker.org/user
  • WANDB_API_KEY: https://wandb.ai/authorize
  • HF_TOKEN: https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens

Then you need to write them in beaker secret as follows (replace the xxxx with your own API key or token) 

beaker_whoami=$(beaker account whoami --format json | jq -r '.[0].name')
beaker secret write -w ai2/tulu-2-improvements "${beaker_whoami}_BEAKER_TOKEN" xxxx
beaker secret write -w ai2/tulu-2-improvements "${beaker_whoami}_WANDB_API_KEY" xxxx
beaker secret write -w ai2/tulu-2-improvements "${beaker_whoami}_HF_TOKEN" xxxx
beaker secret write -w ai2/tulu-3-dev "${beaker_whoami}_BEAKER_TOKEN" xxxx
beaker secret write -w ai2/tulu-3-dev "${beaker_whoami}_WANDB_API_KEY" xxxx
beaker secret write -w ai2/tulu-3-dev "${beaker_whoami}_HF_TOKEN" xxxx

docs.title: mason.py (for job submission)
docs.text:
mason.py is our job submission script. It basically takes your command and runs it in the specified clusters.

For example, let's say you have a training job like this:

python open_instruct/finetune.py \
    --model_name_or_path EleutherAI/pythia-14m \
    --tokenizer_name EleutherAI/pythia-14m \
    --dataset_mixer_list allenai/tulu-3-sft-personas-algebra 100 \
    --with_tracking --report_to wandb

You can take your command above and run it on the weka cluster with the following command (use -- to separate the mason command from the python command):

python mason.py \
    --cluster ai2/jupiter ai2/saturn ai2/neptune \
    --workspace ai2/tulu-3-dev \
    --image nathanl/open_instruct_auto --pure_docker_mode \
    --priority normal \
    --budget ai2/oe-adapt \
    --gpus 0 -- python open_instruct/finetune.py \
    --model_name_or_path EleutherAI/pythia-14m \
    --tokenizer_name EleutherAI/pythia-14m \
    --dataset_mixer_list allenai/tulu-3-sft-personas-algebra 100 \
    --with_tracking --report_to wandb

docs.title: Choosing how the job is scheduled
docs.text: Pass --min_runtime with the time the job needs to reach a checkpoint (e.g. --min_runtime 2h), plus --auto_resume if Beaker should requeue it after preemption. On allocation-scheduled clusters this makes the job allocated: it queues ahead of backfill and is protected until its min runtime ends, and shorter min runtimes schedule sooner. Your workspace needs an allocation on that cluster, or Beaker rejects the job at submission. The legacy --preemptible runs only as backfill and may wait indefinitely, and passing neither flag, as in the example above, requests an 8-hour protected job, the hardest kind to schedule. Run python mason.py --help for details.

docs.title: What mason.py does automatically
docs.text:
Auto set HF cache environment variables:

During the job submission, it automatically tries to setup a shared Hugging Face cache with environment variables. For example, it sets

  • HF_HOME=/weka/oe-adapt-default/allennlp/.cache/huggingface.
  • HF_DATASETS_CACHE=/weka/oe-adapt-default/allennlp/.cache/huggingface
  • HF_HUB_CACHE=/weka/oe-adapt-default/allennlp/.cache/hub

Auto set --hf_entity and --wandb_entity arguments:

so during runtime we issue fewer HF API calls, which sometimes could fail due to rate limiting.

Auto caching datasets:

mason.py will auto call --cache_dataset_only for you, so you do the tokenization locally instead of in the jobs, which saves idle GPU time in the actual jobs.

docs.title: Ai2 Internal Evaluation
docs.text:
We provide a script integrated with beaker for use internally at Ai2. There are couple of use cases.

1. Run evals against a public Hugging Face model. Basically you need to prefix the model name with hf- and provide the location as the HF path (e.g. meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct).

for model in allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-DPO allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-SFT allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-SFT allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924-Instruct; do
python scripts/submit_eval_jobs.py \
    --model_name hf-$model \
    --cluster ai2/jupiter ai2/neptune ai2/saturn ai2/ceres  \
    --priority high \
    --location $model \
    --is_tuned \
    --workspace "tulu-3-results" \
    --priority high \
    --preemptible \
    --use_hf_tokenizer_template \
    --run_oe_eval_experiments \
    --evaluate_on_weka \
    --skip_oi_evals
done

2. Run evals against a model hosted on Beaker dataset. If it's a training run, you should try matching the exp_name and run_id with the training run.

model_name=0222_32B_dpo_lr_8.5e-7__allenai_open_instruct_dev__42__1741225304
url=https://wandb.ai/ai2-llm/open_instruct_internal/runs/7afq8x28
location=01JNMHSM8DDSFB3GJDBM5MP6J8
python scripts/submit_eval_jobs.py \
    --model_name $model_name \
    --cluster ai2/jupiter ai2/neptune ai2/saturn ai2/ceres  \
    --priority high \
    --location $location \
    --is_tuned \
    --workspace "tulu-3-results" \
    --preemptible \
    --use_hf_tokenizer_template \
    --run_oe_eval_experiments \
    --skip_oi_evals \
    --run_id $url

This will later show up in the internal leaderboard.

3. Run evals against a model hosted on weka.

python scripts/submit_eval_jobs.py \
    --model_name test_no_hf_upload \
    --location /weka/oe-adapt-default/costah/models/0129_grpo_math_kl_fix_zs_0.0_16_half-m_461_checkpoints/step_640 \
    --cluster ai2/saturn ai2/neptune \
    --is_tuned \
    --workspace "tulu-3-results" \
    --priority high \
    --preemptible \
    --use_hf_tokenizer_template \
    --beaker_image "nathanl/open_instruct_auto" \
    --run_oe_eval_experiments \
    --evaluate_on_weka \
    --oe_eval_tasks gsm8k::tulu,minerva_math::tulu \
    --run_id https://wandb.ai/ai2-llm/open_instruct_internal/runs/swf79vby \
    --skip_oi_evals \
    --oe_eval_max_length 8096

4. Run evals against a model on Google Cloud Storage.

python scripts/submit_eval_jobs.py \
    --model_name test_gs_location \
    --location gs://ai2-llm/post-training/allenai/Llama-3.1-Tulu-3.1-8B \
    --cluster ai2/jupiter \
    --is_tuned \
    --workspace tulu-3-results \
    --preemptible \
    --use_hf_tokenizer_template \
    --beaker_image nathanl/open_instruct_auto \
    --oe_eval_tasks gsm8k::tulu \
    --skip_oi_evals \
    --gpu_multiplier 2 \
    --run_oe_eval_experiments

docs.title: Running with gantry
docs.text:
You can also run with gantry, if you want to test changes. Important: Before you run any command with gantry, make sure you commit and push, since gantry will attempt to clone the repo with your local latest commit hash.

See the "One-Time Setup" section below before running commands. To test your setup, run the following command -- if this job succeeds, then you're ready to run evaluations with gantry.

gantry run --workspace {workspace} --budget ai2/oe-adapt --beaker-image kavelr/oe-safety --venv base --cluster ai2/jupiter --env-secret OPENAI_API_KEY=openai_api_key --env-secret HF_TOKEN=hf_token -- python -c 'print("Hello world")'

You can freely add any additional arguments to give to Beaker, such as a --priority tag which can be set to preemptible, normal, high, or urgent. AI2 policies may restrict the priorities that are available to users on certain clusters.

In the examples below, text within {} tags should be replaced with your own values.

As a convenience, you can use the evaluation/gantry_run.sh script which includes some necessary arguments. You can use it the same way as gantry run, but excluding these boilerplate arguments (take a look at the script to see what it includes). Example usage:

PYTHONPATH=safety-eval ./evaluation/gantry_run.sh --workspace {workspace} --cluster {cluster} --gpus {n_gpus} \
    --priority {priority} -- python evaluation/run_all_generation_benchmarks.py \
    --model_name_or_path allenai/tulu-2-dpo-7b \
    --model_input_template_path_or_name tulu2 \
    --report_output_path /results/metrics.json

docs.title: Extra Beaker Commands
docs.text:
Here is an example using the full gantry run command. Use the beaker image seungjuh/oe-safety-support-olmo17

Important: Please include all the beaker arguments exactly as in the examples unless intentionally modifying some configuration. Many of them are necessary to avoid job failures, such as --beaker-image, --venv, and --env-secret. Note that openai_api_key and hf_token are Beaker workspace secret names, so should not be replaced with actual values (see One-Time Setup).

Note that the -- divides the gantry command from the evaluation command - you can edit the second part to run whatever eval suite you want from the eval.py script. Any additional Beaker arguments such as a dataset mount to use a model from a Beaker dataset or adding a priority tag can be added before the --.

You can also run all generator evaluations parallelized across the GPUs allocated to your batch job, like so: 

gantry run --workspace {your_workspace} --cluster {cluster} --gpus {n_gpus} \
    --name {beaker_experiment_name} --task-name {beaker_task_name} --beaker-image seungjuh/oe-safety-support-olmo17 --venv base \
    --env-secret OPENAI_API_KEY=openai_api_key \
    --env-secret HF_TOKEN=hf_token \
    --budget {budget} -- python evaluation/run_all_generation_benchmarks.py \
    --model_name_or_path allenai/tulu-2-dpo-7b \
    --model_input_template_path_or_name tulu2 \
    --report_output_path /results/metrics.json --save_individual_results_path /results/all.json

Because the --report_output_path argument is set to /results/metrics.json, the output will automatically get logged to Beaker metrics in the experiment page (example).

docs.title: Common Gotchas
docs.text:
If you're experiencing job failures, here are some things to check:

  • Make sure your local changes are committed, pushed, and up to date with the remote
  • Make sure you have --beaker-image seungjuh/oe-safety-support-olmo17 and --venv base in your gantry run command
  • Check your GitHub personal access token is authorized to access the allenai organization
  • Make sure the openai_api_key and hf_token secrets exist in your Beaker workspace

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Our setup mostly follows our Dockerfile, which uses Python 3.10. Note that Open Instruct is a research codebase and does not guarantee backward compatibility. We offer two installation strategies:

  • Local installation: This is the recommended way to install Open Instruct. You can install the dependencies by running the following commands: 

    pip install --upgrade pip "setuptools<70.0.0" wheel
# TODO, unpin setuptools when this issue in flash attention is resolved
pip install torch==2.5.1 torchvision==0.20.1 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121
pip install packaging
pip install flash-attn==2.7.2.post1 --no-build-isolation
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .
python -m nltk.downloader punkt

  • Local installation with uv (preview): We are experimenting with using uv. You can install via 

    uv sync
uv sync --extra compile # to install flash attention

  • Docker installation: You can also use the Dockerfile to build a Docker image. You can build the image with the following command:

docker build . -t open_instruct_dev
# if you are interally at AI2, you can create an image like this:
beaker_user=$(beaker account whoami --format json | jq -r '.[0].name')
beaker image delete $beaker_user/open_instruct_dev
beaker image create open_instruct_dev -n open_instruct_dev -w ai2/$beaker_user

Optionally you can build the base image with the following command:

docker build --build-arg CUDA=12.1.0 --build-arg TARGET=cudnn8-devel --build-arg DIST=ubuntu20.04 -f  Dockerfile.base . -t cuda-no-conda:12.1-cudnn8-dev-ubuntu20.04
  • Docker with uv: You can also use the Dockerfile to build a Docker image with uv. You can build the image with the following command:
docker build -f Dockerfile.uv --build-arg UV_CACHE_DIR=$UV_CACHE_DIR -t open_instruct_dev_uv .
# if you are interally at AI2, you can create an image like this:
beaker_user=$(beaker account whoami --format json | jq -r '.[0].name')
beaker image delete $beaker_user/open_instruct_dev_uv
beaker image create open_instruct_dev_uv -n open_instruct_dev_uv -w ai2/$beaker_user

If you are internally at AI2, you may launch experiments using our always-up-to-date auto-built image nathanl/open_instruct_auto.

docs.title: MILES GRPO documentation
docs.text:
Use python -m open_instruct.miles for new GRPO work with supported Olmo MoE models. Open Instruct owns the researcher configuration and data/reward integration; MILES owns rollout orchestration and shared RL machinery; the adapter trains through OLMo-core and serves through SGLang. Check model and workload support below.

The grpo.py Core/vLLM and grpo_fast.py DeepSpeed/vLLM entry points remain current alternatives for dense-model training, existing workflows and historical reproduction. See their GRPO guide for configuration and launch recipes. MILES also provides a dense Olmo 3 adapter, but that path is less extensively validated; consult model support when choosing a backend. Introducing MILES does not deprecate the existing GRPO trainers.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
1. Start with the MILES GRPO guide for setup, the runtime image and a first run.
  2. Check support and limits, model support and topology, and read the development defaults.
  3. Copy a structured example.
  4. Read the workflow, then follow the launch guide for your host. Planning does not require GPUs or mounted checkpoints.
  5. Use operations to check completion and inspect run artifacts.

docs.title: Authority and maintenance
docs.text:
Current instructions live in this directory. Example TOMLs express starting recipes. Configuration code, the pinned native parser snapshot, and runtime/miles/runtime.lock.json define accepted settings and runtime provenance.

Maintain the generated reference with python -m scripts.miles.generate_docs and check it with python -m scripts.miles.generate_docs --check. See development for validation.

See publication modes for current mixed-policy refresh, barrier controls and independent engine drain.

docs.title: Architecture and development
docs.text:
The public entrypoint is python -m open_instruct.miles. Its structured RunSpec compiles into a RunConfig containing CoreConfig and native MILES options. The Python API is available for integrations; use the structured workflow when preparation, placement and submission should come from one file.

Layer Owns Open Instruct wrapper Config validation, preparation, verifiers, launch/receipts, run artifacts MILES runtime Rollout actors, SGLang engines, sample/advantage/loss machinery, shared transport helpers Core adapter (in MILES) Model construction, document/replay alignment, scoring/training forward, gradient synchronization, optimizer/checkpoints and tensor export OLMo-core Model and distributed-training primitives, attention/expert execution olmo-sglang Serving architecture registration and model-specific execution

The Core actor at miles.backends.core_utils.actor.OLMoCoreTrainRayActor implements the MILES trainer boundary. Its model/checkpoint code and publication machinery live in the pinned MILES fork. The driver coordinates collections, optimization and versioned weight publication. Dense standard-model support is isolated from the specialized MoE path. Implementation contracts describe the detailed lifecycle and packing describes document/routing alignment.

docs.title: Runtime sources and images
docs.text:
runtime/miles/runtime.lock.json is the source of truth for exact dependency commits and the immutable binary base. Builds fetch those commits without patches or moving branch tips. MILES uses the organized adapter hooks; OLMo-core provides the model, objective and checkpoint APIs required by this adapter; olmo-sglang supplies compatible serving models. The ordinary Open Instruct environment keeps its own dependency versions.

The MILES pin includes the v0.1.2 async-consumer compatibility fix from miles-olmo-core PR #10. Its refresh and engine-drain dequeues accept the native consumer's optional trainer identity and preserve Core's explicit rejection of multi-policy training.

The binary base contains the compiled dependencies, including FA2, FA3 and FA4. It excludes the MILES, Core, SGLang and Open Instruct source overlays. Application builds add locked source repositories as runtime-base, then the committed Open Instruct checkout as application. They do not compile FlashAttention, even without a local Docker cache. Source-only lock changes rebuild source layers; binary dependency changes require a new base. Editable installs still fetch build-system dependencies such as setuptools and pybind11, and Megatron builds a small C++ dataset helper. Those build-tool requirements are not fully pinned; the source and base pins do not make application builds bit-for-bit reproducible.

The selected base is Beaker 01M5ZYQZVF7DDJ1VR619KRSS42 (robertb/miles-binary-base-20261027), Docker sha256:947e615f93cb88f8739ba270f30adc7f012af8bc0abf43e96f11cd5d3b2d6354. Its package versions, CPU imports and source isolation were checked, and a pull by immutable ID reproduced the same Docker ID. The single-GPU Core RL smoke passed on application image 01M61Z2XBQB6EP3SJNAX1YN0HV: four optimizer updates, shared-engine evaluations, checkpoints and HF export on Holmes. This tiny-model check uses Torch attention; it does not qualify every FlashAttention backend or a Qwen OPD GPU training run with the public Megatron sources. The application image (robertb/miles-main-smoke-5a7be0398) was built from 5a7be0398e8244cd5376983427e57d4deeea2e39, Docker sha256:83cc907a035f98ba69d3b8b7eaaaaa7477d1c06c6efca39da4414ef174df3c67, and includes the current public source lock and review cleanup.

A CPU-only runtime-base rebuild from commit 3563eb52ac4b02d731786e8f1a4e39a52951f2a2 is published as Beaker image 01M61YFEWE1BATA8KQ4VAV2DY8 (robertb/miles-runtime-base-3563eb52a), Docker sha256:f97469549508d2af9896161889cc45060c52ece5743ecfcbe937039d3043b784. Its packaged lock matches the current lock, all six source checkouts match their pinned revisions without patches, and serving/attention CPU imports passed. This records CPU build verification of the runtime sources separately from the application-image GPU smoke above, which subsequently verified the same source lock.

The source layer includes Megatron-LM from the Radix fork, pinned to 235952df607b3820716e5e67728a5ab470ca33ae (the previous runtime's revision, including its Qwen3.5 FP32 optimizer fix), rather than the current miles-main tip used by the pinned MILES Dockerfile. Megatron Bridge uses the public Radix revision selected by that Dockerfile. These dependencies support Qwen OPD. The image does not install olmo-megatron, the private Olmo Bridge fork, or Olmo-specific Megatron patches; Olmo training uses the Core backend. Package metadata and entrypoints are installed with --no-deps to preserve the binary stack. /src/Megatron-LM remains a compatibility symlink for the OPD launcher.

EOPD metadata transport is implemented in the pinned MILES source, without a local runtime patch. Open Instruct's opd_hooks stores teacher top-k values in Sample.train_metadata; rollout conversion copies those dictionaries into train_data["metadata"], and the Megatron training step requests metadata from get_batch for the custom loss. This training field is separate from the input dataset metadata selected by --metadata-key.

For ordinary application builds:

python scripts/miles/build_image.py --base-image LOCAL_LOADED_BASE_IMAGE --tag open-instruct:miles-core

Use --target runtime-base to build only the locked dependency sources, without adding the Open Instruct application checkout. The default target is application. The image arguments are local Docker tags loaded on the build host; Beaker names and immutable IDs identify the images to pull before invoking the helper.

All repositories in the runtime lock are public; no GitHub credential is needed for these source fetches. Standalone source preparation can use --cache olmo-sglang=/path/to/clone. Existing published images retain their original sources; rebuild after changing the lock.

prepare_runtime refuses to replace existing source directories. Its --cache arguments can use local clones as fetch sources; they do not select uncommitted sibling code. build_image checks the immutable base Docker ID. For actual submission use the committed-image launcher, not a one-off Beaker command with different mounts or source provenance.

docs.title: Rebuilding the binary base
docs.text:
The reproducible maintainer recipe is runtime/miles/Dockerfile.base; its two immutable inputs are recorded in runtime/miles/base-build.lock.json. Pull both Beaker images into Docker, then run:

python scripts/miles/build_base_image.py \
  --compiled-parent LOCAL_COMPILED_PARENT \
  --flash-attention-builder LOCAL_FA3_BUILDER \
  --tag open-instruct:miles-binary-base

Both Docker IDs are verified, and the parent-image label comes from the same lock. The helper passes the compiler image as FLASH_ATTENTION_BUILDER and the runtime parent as COMPILED_PARENT. Only FA wheels are transferred from the compiler image to the clean compiled parent. FA2/FA4 wheel downloads are checksum-verified; the final stage resets inherited application metadata and entrypoints. This preserves the qualified CUDA/PyTorch stack rather than rebuilding all dependencies from an upstream CUDA distribution. Build on an amd64 Linux host: FA3 compilation defaults to two jobs, with --max-jobs available for hosts with sufficient RAM. The published base's FA3 build took about 31 minutes with eight jobs.

The final environment list was compared with the locked compiled parent. It preserves its runtime settings while dropping legacy OLMO_MILES_* cache and verifier paths. Recheck this list against the parent image whenever changing the parent pin; FROM scratch does not inherit environment variables automatically.

Before changing the pin again, verify CPU imports, an application build and GPU forward/backward and training on the intended hardware. CPU imports alone do not establish GPU correctness.

docs.title: Local development
docs.text:
The ordinary CPU suite covers configuration, planning, launch specifications, rewards, data preparation, rendezvous, heartbeat, recovery and topology contracts without installing MILES or SGLang. The MILES contracts workflow also checks the maintained scripts and checks application types without requiring the private runtime. Recording and summary implementation tests live with their MILES implementation; Open Instruct keeps record configuration tests and runtime selection/buffer integration tests. The moved adapter is checked against that Core API in the dedicated runtime environment; Open Instruct's ordinary type check covers the application integration. The MoE numerical tests deliberately require the Core revision in the runtime lock. The ordinary uv.lock Core version is for existing SFT/DPO paths and is not upgraded to make those runtime-only tests importable.

uv run pytest open_instruct/test_miles*.py

The dedicated runtime suite uses the separate application image. From its /opt/core-rl working directory, run:

bash scripts/miles/test_runtime.sh -q

This command fails if runtime dependencies are missing. Without the explicit runtime flag, ordinary CPU collection omits tests/miles/ when MILES or SGLang is absent. CUDA numerical cases skip when no GPU is visible. A passing CPU run therefore does not check GPU kernels, distributed gradients or publication. The ordinary Open Instruct GPU CI image does not include the private MILES runtime; dedicated runtime checks are a separate maintainer validation step.

For a training lifecycle check, copy dev.toml to runs/, select a compatible tiny checkpoint, and follow the committed-image launcher. Verify the rendered replica group and retain image, config and completion artifacts. Test refresh separately when changing publication behavior; a tiny mechanics check does not establish learning quality.

docs.title: Documentation checks
docs.text:
python -m scripts.miles.generate_docs --check
uv run pytest open_instruct/test_miles_documentation.py
uv run mkdocs build
make style-check
make quality-check

MkDocs generates the four reference pages in memory from configuration sources, the compact pinned parser schema and reviewed reference-help.json descriptions. Neither the pages nor native help are tracked. Ordinary documentation builds and local plan/validate commands need no MILES installation. Without a native help capture, option tables show names, types, choices, restrictions and reviewed supplements; other help and value defaults are explicitly marked unavailable.

When runtime pins change, regenerate the compact schema inside the matching runtime and review its diff:

python -m scripts.miles.snapshot_options open_instruct/miles/configuration/options.json

For full upstream help and parser defaults, capture an artifact in the pinned runtime using a writable checkout, then supply it to the documentation build:

python -m scripts.miles.capture_option_help --image IMMUTABLE_IMAGE_ID --output runs/native-help.json
MILES_NATIVE_HELP=runs/native-help.json uv run mkdocs build

The capture checks the installed parser against the expanded compact schema; the docs build rejects stale hashes or missing actions. Parser defaults are not model-dependent resolved defaults. To inspect Markdown separately, run python -m scripts.miles.generate_docs --output-dir runs/miles-docs (optionally with --native-help runs/native-help.json). --check validates the reference inputs without writing files. Edit source definitions and reviewed descriptions, not generated output. Change maintained examples only as a deliberate recipe change; see development defaults.

docs.title: Type checking the moved adapter
docs.text:
In a development environment with the pinned MILES and Core sources, run:

ty check /path/to/miles/miles/backends/core_utils --extra-search-path /path/to/OLMo-core/src

Open Instruct's CPU checks do not fetch the private MILES repository. The committed application image and runtime tests check both repositories together.

docs.title: Adapter package layout
docs.text:
open_instruct/miles/ groups code by responsibility. The public CLI remains python -m open_instruct.miles; package initializers do not load the GPU runtime.

Package Responsibility configuration RunSpec/CoreConfig, native options, validation, topology and capacity planning execution Preparation, Beaker submission, cluster bootstrap and training coordination MILES backends/core_utils Core actor, model backends, packing, optimizer scheduling, checkpoints and trainer diagnostics rollout Application data-source selection and rollout metrics; managed generation, admission and completed queues live in MILES backends/core_utils/rollout MILES backends/core_utils/publication Weight delivery, engine drain, policy versions and durable policy state rewards Verifiers, reward routing and managed judges datasets Dataset preparation, mixtures, inference records and prompt selection evaluation Background evaluation submission, workers and result publication infrastructure Application artifact publication and bounded infrastructure waits; compiler/HF cache lifecycle lives in MILES

Keep diagnostics next to the component they observe. Keep configuration imports CPU-only, model backends loaded on demand, and package initializers minimal. MILES backends/core_utils/data.py adapts samples to the trainer; rollout/data_source.py owns runtime data-source behavior; datasets/run_data.py prepares researcher inputs.

Python integration imports use these package paths, for example from open_instruct.miles.configuration.run_spec import RunSpec. The pinned AllenAI MILES fork must use the matching trainer and rollout hook paths. Rebuild the application image when updating this layout and its runtime pin together; existing images retain their original code. Custom verifier factories and saved native options must reference these package paths.

The CPU CLI checks in open_instruct/test_miles_package_layout.py run without site-packages. tests/miles/test_package_layout.py resolves hooks supplied by both repositories inside the pinned runtime.

docs.title: Application callbacks and CPU tools
docs.text:
The backend trainer and managed rollout modules do not import Open Instruct. Open Instruct supplies core_records_factory for per-question recording and core_evaluation_snapshot for requested post-update HF exports. Those callbacks preserve the existing recording and evaluation schedules. Dataset preparation, reward callbacks, data-source selection, Beaker launch and evaluation submission remain application-owned. The native olmo_core argument loader still resolves Open Instruct's run configuration; that is an explicit configuration integration.

Small CPU planning and artifact-reader helpers remain local so plan, validate and offline analysis work without the private runtime. Runtime integration tests compare their algorithms with the MILES counterparts: scoring policy, capacity reporting, timeout diagnostics, atomic JSON publication, input validation and throughput arithmetic.

docs.title: Core runtime compatibility
docs.text:
The olmo-core revision in runtime.lock.json is the Core source used by the runtime. The adapter interfaces it relies on were merged in OLMo-core PR #888. The runtime pins merge commit 6ceda6530625caa5d23e3be8a455c600f62a7338, including the reviewed RoPE import fixes, alongside the MILES v0.1.2 integration.

Core's routed-expert match_eager_rounding defaults to false. The pinned MILES adapter explicitly enables it for policy scoring and accepts legacy MILES checkpoint manifests with equivalent scoring semantics. Other Core users keep the default behavior.

Core's PR checks and application validation cover different boundaries. Rebuild runtime/application images from the lock and validate the intended training topology; an existing image retains its original source revisions. Record application validation with the exact image and source pins. The compact options snapshot must be regenerated whenever runtime source pins change.

docs.title: Async queues, capacity, and discarded work
docs.text: The target is continuous useful generation and training. This requires matching rates, not an unlimited queue: if generation is persistently slower the trainer waits; if it is faster, bounded storage eventually pauses submission. A larger buffer absorbs bursts but does not fix a sustained rate mismatch. Publication still pauses the inference fleet; evaluation/shutdown lifecycle drains are separate costs. Queue selection remains FIFO.

docs.title: Where work waits
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    D[Prompt source and retry ledger] --> P[Producer group tasks]
    P --> H[Global generation semaphore]
    H --> S[Router and engine waiting requests]
    S --> G[Engine prefill and decode]
    G --> R[Reward or judge and sibling completion]
    R --> Q[Completed-group FIFO]
    Q --> B[Assemble rollout collection]
    B --> T[Shard, score, and optimize]
    T --> W[Publish weights]
    W --> B
Boundary What limits it What releases capacity Prompt source → producer async_max_concurrent_samples, rounded down to whole groups (at least one group) With rollout_submission_granularity="group", the entire generation-and-reward group must finish. sample backfills when individual sample tasks finish, while still delivering whole groups for training. Producer → generation function A global semaphore of sglang_server_concurrency × engine_count Generation returns; per-sample reward work runs after releasing this semaphore. Router → engine execution Each engine's sglang_max_running_requests, token/state pools, scheduling and routing Requests finish or the scheduler changes their running/waiting status. The configured request maximum is not a guarantee of actual running capacity. Responses → completed group All siblings and required rewards must finish The group becomes eligible for the completed buffer. Judge services can have their own concurrency limits. Completed group → FIFO floor(async_data_buffer_capacity_factor × rollout_batch_size) groups Training dequeues a group or a stale group is discarded. FIFO → collection rollout_batch_size eligible whole groups The collection is assembled, then converted/sharded for the trainer. There is no separate deep queue of already assembled trainer batches in this driver. Collection → optimizer global_batch_size, plus trainer topology and microbatching Optimizer steps complete. A collection can contain multiple optimizer batches where the selected mode allows it. Refresh currently requires one.

A full completed buffer blocks the producer's insertion of a completion and hence new submissions. Other requests already submitted can still finish. Completed results can therefore also reside in producer tasks waiting to be inserted: the FIFO's reported capacity is not a bound on all resident response data. Lifecycle drains temporarily reserve additional space for already-owned completions.

In group mode, ownership ends after successful FIFO insertion. Thus producer ownership and completed-buffer occupancy are separate: a 64-sample producer plus 32-sample FIFO can retain 96 future samples while the trainer processes its current batch. At batch 32 and lag two, a fast generator can make more same-policy work than the next two updates can consume. Planning warns about this combined headroom. It is an upper bound, not a predicted discard rate: generation times, refresh boundaries and ongoing consumption determine actual age.

The limits are independent.
